definition.text: The branch of practical philosophy that sets out the kinds of argument that can be made for protecting nature and using natural resources sustainably.

facts.text: Its main competing views are anthropocentrism, ecocentrism (physiocentrism) and theocentrism.
It asks questions such as whether forests should be clear-cut for human consumption and which species should be valued for their own sake.
It influences environmental law, sociology, ecotheology, ecological economics, ecology and geography.
The field grew in response to Rachel Carson, Murray Bookchin and the first Earth Day in 1970.
Lynn White's 1967 paper on the roots of the ecological crisis and Garrett Hardin's 1968 'Tragedy of the Commons' had a crucial impact.
Alan Marshall sorts its approaches into libertarian extension, ecologic extension and conservation ethics.
Animal ethics and environmental ethics clash over duties to wild animals; some see them as incompatible, others as reconcilable.

definition.text: The view that the environment has intrinsic value: it is valuable in itself, not just for its use to people.

facts.text: Arne Næss coined 'deep ecology' in 1972, arguing that all non-human entities have intrinsic value.
Marshall's libertarian extension, under which it falls, extends equal rights to all members of a community that includes non-humans.
Defenders of deep ecology criticised John Passmore's early environmental ethics for its anthropocentrism.

definition.text: An approach to environmental ethics that stresses the interdependence and diversity of living things and gives intrinsic value to whole ecosystems.

facts.text: It is a scientific reflection on nature, where libertarian extension is a political one.
James Lovelock's Gaia hypothesis, treating Earth as one whole with its own ethical value, may belong here.

definition.text: Valuing the environment only for its usefulness to people, and protecting it as a means to human welfare.

facts.text: Because it rejects deep ecology's intrinsic value, it is often called 'shallow ecology'.
It may underlie government positions at the 1992 Rio Earth Summit and the 1997 Kyoto summit.

definition.text: How the main theories of right action, consequentialism, deontology and virtue ethics, are used to reason about the environment.

facts.text: Consequentialism judges actions by their results, such as whether they maximise well-being, which treats nature instrumentally.
Deontology says intrinsically valuable things must be protected as ends in themselves, so damaging nature is wrong in itself, not just a net loss.
Virtue ethics asks which character traits to cultivate, which avoids defining intrinsic value but is arguably anthropocentric.

definition.text: The position that humans are the most important element in any situation and must always be their own main concern.

facts.text: In environmental ethics it is often seen as the root cause of problems humans create in the ecosphere.
Critics say people judge the environment and other organisms by their usefulness to humans.
Many argue environmental studies should assess the intrinsic value of non-human beings.

title: Value of Earth

definition.text: The net worth of the planet, a disputed idea both in what 'value' means and in what counts as 'Earth'.

facts.text: It is usually equated with the total value of all ecosystem services.
A 1997 estimate put ecosystem services at $33 trillion a year, with a range of $16 trillion to $54 trillion.
Against a combined world GNP of about $18 trillion, that implied ecosystems provide 1.8 times as much value as people create.
A later estimate gave $125 trillion a year for 2011, twice world GDP, with yearly losses of 4.3–20.2 trillion.

contested_note: Critics questioned the 1997 figures, especially the GNP comparison, though they accepted the basic approach.

conflicts.text: Combined world GNP closer to $28 trillion, making ecosystem services only 1.2 times as valuable.
conflicts.note: Disputes the $18 trillion GNP figure used in the 1997 comparison.

conflicts.text: World Bank total GDP in 1997 of $31 trillion, about equal to the ecosystem value.
conflicts.note: GDP rather than GNP; another benchmark for the same comparison.

title: Value pluralism

definition.text: The idea that there are several basic values that can all be right and yet conflict with one another.

facts.text: Conflicting values are often held to be incommensurable, with no objective ranking of their importance.
It opposes value monism, which says all values can be measured on or reduced to a single scale.
Unlike relativism, it accepts limits, such as when vital human needs are violated.
Isaiah Berlin first popularised a substantial account of it.
Alan Brown objects that values are commensurable because they can be compared by their contribution to human good.
Social ecological economics builds value incommensurability and value pluralism into its approach.

contested_note: Critics such as Alan Brown and Ronald Dworkin reject the claim that conflicting values cannot be compared.
